system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2154-03-23 18:46:00 to 2154-03-26 16:23:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for left flank pain lasting 15 days, with a history of chronic myeloid leukemia, chronic graft-versus-host disease, and prior anticoagulant use. Imaging revealed subacute fractures in the left ribs, likely due to a previous fall, which explained the pain. A new soft tissue nodule in the right breast was incidentally found on CT and recommended for mammographic follow-up. The patient also reported bilateral leg pain with ambulation, suggestive of claudication, prompting a recommendation for outpatient ankle-brachial index testing. Pain was managed with oxycodone and gabapentin, and prednisone was tapered to 30 mg daily. The patient remained stable, with no acute abdominal process, and was discharged home with follow-up plans.
problems: Other (abnormal) findings on radiological examination of breast
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Unspecified hemorrhoids without mention of complication
Gastric ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Rivera. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having bad headaches, stomach pain, and my right calf has been hurting again. It’s been getting worse over the past few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had chronic graft-versus-host disease for a few years now. Are these symptoms different from usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The headaches are new—constant and all over my head. My stomach pain is dull but never goes away, and I had one episode of vomiting before coming in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check things out. Your vitals are stable, and your exam shows mild belly tenderness and some calf tenderness. We’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re ordering a CT of your head and abdomen to make sure there’s nothing serious going on. We’ll also check your blood work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT head showed a tiny spot in the left thalamus, but it’s likely not dangerous. No stroke or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that what’s causing the headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but it might just be an old change. Your neck exam shows muscle tightness and limited movement. That’s more likely the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had neck pain for years, but this headache is different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: True, but your MRI of the neck shows only mild arthritis, no pinched nerves. We think the headache is from muscle spasms. We’ll try a muscle relaxer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my stomach pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT of your abdomen was clear—no blockages, infections, or new issues. You have a known gastric ulcer, so we think that’s the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on omeprazole. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll keep you on omeprazole and Zantac. Your pain has improved since admission, which supports this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my leg? I’m worried it’s another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your Lovenox level. It was low when you came in, which suggests it wasn’t fully effective. But your ultrasound didn’t show a new clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could I have missed a dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll keep you on Lovenox for now, but your team may switch you to warfarin if they can monitor your INR reliably at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your blood results. Your liver enzymes are still a bit high, which fits with your GVHD. But your kidney function is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low, but stable. Platelets are normal. Your leukemia remains in remission, which is great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What about the diabetes? My last A1c was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your A1c was 7.5%. Given your steroid use, we think it’s steroid-induced. We’re starting you on 10 units of NPH insulin at breakfast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken insulin before. Is it hard?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have a nurse teach you how to inject it. It’s simple, and it helps match your prednisone peak. You’ll follow up with endocrinology soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your headaches have improved, and your belly pain is almost gone. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The muscle relaxer helps. But I still get tightness in my neck at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding a soft neck collar for nighttime. It may help reduce strain. Also, your rapamycin level was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be why I felt so tired and achy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. High levels can cause fatigue and joint pain. We’re lowering your dose from 2 mg to 1.5 mg daily. We’ll check it again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been skipping my eye drops because I’m scared of cataracts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your eye GVHD needs treatment. Please resume the drops. Your ophthalmologist will monitor for cataracts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your symptoms have improved, and no serious causes were found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking omeprazole and Zantac for your stomach. Use the muscle relaxer as needed. Wear the neck collar at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, start the NPH insulin at breakfast. A nurse will go over it with you. Also, keep taking Lovenox daily unless your doctor says otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. Your follow-up appointments are set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: With oncology and eye doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and endocrinology for your diabetes. Call us if headaches or stomach pain return, or if you have swelling in your leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Keep up with your meds, and we’ll keep monitoring your GVHD and rapamycin level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take them as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for worsening headaches, abdominal pain, and right calf pain. Imaging showed no acute intracranial or abdominal pathology; the headache was attributed to neck muscle spasms, and abdominal pain was likely due to a gastric ulcer. Her rapamycin level was elevated, prompting a dose reduction. Diabetes was diagnosed with an A1c of 7.5%, likely steroid-induced, and NPH insulin was initiated. Symptoms improved during the stay, and she was discharged home with updated medications and follow-up plans for oncology, ophthalmology, and endocrinology.
